## Before you start

::: {.callout-note}
Hit the **Run Code** button to run the code in a cell. To run only part of a cell, highlight the lines you want and press **Cmd + Return** (Mac) or **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows). All code cells on this page share the same R session, so an object you create in one cell is still available in the next one.
:::

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true

library(jsonlite)
```

This page revisits the JSON lecture topic by topic. For the conceptual points, try to answer the question yourself before opening the *Solution* tab. For the coding points, first write something in the *Try it* tab, then compare it with the *Solution* tab — the code there is folded by default, so you are not spoiled unless you click to open it.

## 1. What does "JSON" stand for?

JSON stands for *JavaScript Object Notation*. Even though the name references JavaScript, JSON itself is a language-independent, plain-text format.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
JSON = **J**ava**S**cript **O**bject **N**otation. It is standardized in IETF RFC 8259 and ECMA-404, and can be read and written from R, Python, JavaScript, and many other languages.
:::

Try it yourself: use `jsonlite::fromJSON()` to parse a tiny JSON object and see what kind of R object comes out of it.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

json_text <- '{"language": "JavaScript Object Notation"}'

# parse json_text with fromJSON() and inspect the result

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

json_text <- '{"language": "JavaScript Object Notation"}'

parsed <- jsonlite::fromJSON(json_text)
parsed
class(parsed)
```

:::

## 2. Basic characteristics of JSON

Which of the following statements are correct?

- JSON is a text syntax suitable for the interchange of semi-structured data.
- JSON is standardized, among others, in IETF RFC 8259.
- JSON can only be used together with the JavaScript programming language.
- JSON has many parallels to XML.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The first, second and fourth statements are **true**. The third is **false**: JSON is language-independent, despite the name.
:::

Try it yourself: use `jsonlite::validate()` to check whether a piece of text is actually valid JSON.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

candidate <- '{"Operator": "DVB", "LineNr": "85"}'

# check whether candidate is valid JSON

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

candidate <- '{"Operator": "DVB", "LineNr": "85"}'

jsonlite::validate(candidate)
```

:::

## 3. JSON value types

The JSON standard defines exactly five kinds of values: object, array, number, string, and the three literal names `true`, `false`, `null`. There is no separate "date" type — dates are simply stored as strings.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Object, array, number, string, and the literals `true`/`false`/`null`. "Date" is *not* a JSON value type.
:::

Try it yourself: build an R list mixing several of these value types and convert it to JSON with `toJSON()`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

my_list <- list(
  # add elements of different types here, e.g. a number, a string, a boolean, NULL
)

# convert my_list to JSON

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

my_list <- list(
  line_nr  = 85,
  operator = "DVB",
  active   = TRUE,
  reason   = NA
)

jsonlite::toJSON(my_list, auto_unbox = TRUE, null = "null", na = "null", pretty = TRUE)
```

:::

## 4. Object syntax

An object is wrapped in curly brackets `{ }` and holds zero or more name-value pairs, each name being a string, with a colon between name and value and a comma between pairs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Curly brackets, string names, `:` between name and value, `,` between pairs — and a value can itself be another object or an array.
:::

Try it yourself: turn a named R list into a JSON object and check that the result starts with `{` and ends with `}`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

stop_info <- list(name = "Helmholtzstraße", place = "Dresden", id = "33000742")

# convert stop_info into a JSON object

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

stop_info <- list(name = "Helmholtzstraße", place = "Dresden", id = "33000742")

jsonlite::toJSON(stop_info, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
```

:::

## 5. Array syntax

An array is wrapped in square brackets `[ ]` and holds zero or more values, separated by commas — no names involved, and the values do not have to share the same type.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Square brackets, comma-separated values, no names, and mixed types are allowed.
:::

Try it yourself: convert a plain R vector into a JSON array.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

route_stops <- c("Striesen Niederwaldplatz", "Löbtau Süd", "Mohorner Str.")

# convert route_stops into a JSON array

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

route_stops <- c("Striesen Niederwaldplatz", "Löbtau Süd", "Mohorner Str.")

jsonlite::toJSON(route_stops, pretty = TRUE)
```

:::

## 6. Number syntax

A JSON number may start with a minus sign and may include an exponent (`e`/`E`). Its fractional part is separated by a **dot**, not a comma, and it may not have leading zeros (except the single zero right before a decimal point).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`-4.5E-3` is valid. `4,5` (comma as decimal separator) and `007` (leading zeros) are **not** valid JSON numbers.
:::

Try it yourself: use `validate()` to check a JSON array that contains a number with a leading zero.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

with_leading_zero <- "[007, 1.5, -4.5E-3]"

# check whether this is valid JSON, then try fixing it

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

with_leading_zero <- "[007, 1.5, -4.5E-3]"
jsonlite::validate(with_leading_zero)

fixed <- "[7, 1.5, -4.5E-3]"
jsonlite::validate(fixed)
```

:::

## 7. String syntax

A JSON string always uses **double** quotation marks. Certain characters (like `"` and `\`) must be escaped with a backslash, and any Unicode code point can be written as a hexadecimal escape sequence such as `\u0041`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Double quotes only; `\"` and `\\` are escaped characters; `\u0041` decodes to the letter `A`.
:::

Try it yourself: decode a string containing a Unicode escape sequence.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

escaped <- '["\\u0041", "Hello Dresden!"]'

# parse escaped and see what the first element turns into

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

escaped <- '["\\u0041", "Hello Dresden!"]'
jsonlite::fromJSON(escaped)
```

:::

## 8. Find the errors

Look at this JSON text describing two bus trips:

```
[
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": Stadtbus,
    "LineNr": "85",
  }
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": "Stadtbus",
    "LineNr": 85
  }
]
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Three real problems: `Stadtbus` is missing quotation marks, there is a trailing comma after `"LineNr": "85"`, and there is no comma between the two objects inside the array. `"LineNr": 85` without quotes in the second object is *not* an error — numbers are never quoted in JSON.
:::

Try it yourself: confirm with `validate()` that the broken text is invalid, then fix it.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

broken <- '[
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": Stadtbus,
    "LineNr": "85",
  }
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": "Stadtbus",
    "LineNr": 85
  }
]'

# check broken with validate(), then write a corrected version

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

broken <- '[
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": Stadtbus,
    "LineNr": "85",
  }
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": "Stadtbus",
    "LineNr": 85
  }
]'
jsonlite::validate(broken)

fixed <- '[
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": "Stadtbus",
    "LineNr": "85"
  },
  {
    "Operator": "DVB",
    "Vehicle": "Stadtbus",
    "LineNr": 85
  }
]'
jsonlite::validate(fixed)
jsonlite::fromJSON(fixed)
```

:::

## 9. A genuine limitation of JSON

JSON has no built-in way to represent infinity or "not a number" (NaN) — unlike, say, nested/hierarchical data, which it handles just fine through objects and arrays.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
No representation for `Inf`/`NaN` is a real limitation. Nested data, optional schemas, and human readability are *not* limitations of JSON.
:::

Try it yourself: see what happens when you try to convert `NaN` and `Inf` to JSON with `toJSON()`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

values <- c(1, NaN, Inf, -Inf)

# convert values to JSON and see how NaN/Inf are handled

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

values <- c(1, NaN, Inf, -Inf)

jsonlite::toJSON(values)
```

Notice that `jsonlite` falls back to representing `NaN` and `Inf` as the strings `"NaN"`/`"Inf"` — a workaround, since JSON itself has no native concept for them.

:::

## 10. JSON vs. XML

Both formats are human-readable, hierarchical, and text-based, and are used for similar purposes. The main differences: JSON values are unnamed unless inside an object (every XML element has a name), the same data is usually smaller in JSON than in XML, and XML is designed to be extensible while JSON's grammar is deliberately minimal.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
True: readability/hierarchy, naming difference, XML extensibility vs. JSON simplicity. False: XML is *not* typically more compact than JSON for the same data.
:::

## 11. The R package used for JSON

`jsonlite` offers a bidirectional mapping between JSON and many R data types, and is what we use for reading, writing, and validating JSON in R.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`jsonlite`, with functions like `read_json()`, `toJSON()`, `fromJSON()`, and `validate()`.
:::

Try it yourself: check which version of `jsonlite` is loaded in this session.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

# print the installed version of jsonlite

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

packageVersion("jsonlite")
```

:::

## 12. JSON Schema and related formats

A JSON Schema describes the expected structure of a JSON text (required fields, types, ...) and validating against it returns `TRUE`/`FALSE`. YAML is a **superset** of JSON (every valid JSON text is valid YAML, not the other way around), and GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for geographic features that can be read directly with `sf::st_read()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
True: schema defines structure, validation returns TRUE/FALSE, GeoJSON + `sf::st_read()`. False: YAML is a superset, not a subset, of JSON.
:::

Try it yourself: parse a tiny GeoJSON snippet and see how many features it contains.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Try it

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false

geojson_text <- '{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Dresdner Heide"}},
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Großer Garten"}}
  ]
}'

# parse geojson_text and find out how many features it has

```

## Solution

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: false
#| code-fold: true

geojson_text <- '{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Dresdner Heide"}},
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Großer Garten"}}
  ]
}'

parsed <- jsonlite::fromJSON(geojson_text)
nrow(parsed$features)
parsed$features$properties
```

:::
